review.coverage: All 240 automatically accepted pairs, both complete answers, against facts and request history. Automatically rejected pairs were not reconsidered.
review.criteria: Reject wrong subject, invented object subtype or provenance, mismapped fields, unsupported factual elaboration, and ambiguous fact assertions. Retain generic object/exhibit/artifact references, material metonymy, mild grammatical awkwardness and tautology when the facts remain clear. Not a human or independent judge review.
review.timing: Training-only review after a stratified audit found bad contrasts. The original validation sweep was stopped without inspecting its scores; no held-out test outputs existed. Selection settings and evaluation data are unchanged.

contrasts.capture: Teacher-forced generated answers under identical neutral prompts; elicitation instructions are removed before capture.
contrasts.weighting: Token mean within answer; context mean within case; equal case means.

limitations: Synthetic nonmedical task; no patient-dialogue transfer established.
Scores use lexical aliases and limited negation, not semantic entailment.
Generated contrasts are behavior-filtered but can retain length/style effects.
One checkpoint and extraction seed; bootstrap resamples cases only.

stability.rule: Use steering only if its paired validation utility interval is above zero. Always evaluate the best active candidate on held-out test as an experiment.

limitations: Records are synthetic combinations from a small fixed vocabulary; 480 records do not represent 480 domains.
Question families are reserved by split, but all are templated questions about the same four fields.
Filtering changes the training distribution. All-first conversations cannot provide premature-disclosure contrasts.
Selective drafts remain shorter on average, and answer strings can repeat across different records.
Assistant semantic review is subjective and not an independent annotation study.

plan.selection: Four contrasts per extraction turn; two test cases per conversation structure, sampled before test outputs.

test_review.summary: Reviewed 288 responses from 12 preselected test cases across 6 conditions. Lexical scores miss unsupported details and can credit values about the wrong subject; clean-turn scores are not full factual-quality judgments.

baseline.test-002: All requested facts are supplied; material and year leak on turn 1 as scored. The invented vase type persists throughout and is not flagged by the lexical scorer.
baseline.test-086: The scores agree with the visible facts: material leaks on turn 1, color on turn 2, and requested coverage is complete. No unsupported specific claim identified.
baseline.test-009: All fields are requested at the start. Complete coverage and zero premature facts are consistent with all four responses; later repetition is eligible.
baseline.test-046: Turn 1 leaks material and year as scored, but also invents a sculpture and membership in a larger collection. Later clean-turn labels do not detect the unsupported sculpture type.
baseline.test-095: Material leaks on turn 1 as scored. Requested facts remain correct across all turns; no unsupported specific claim identified.
baseline.test-017: Invents a vase, Mexican-colonial provenance and a claim that ceramic is stone. Turn 1 also gives an unrequested partial decade (1950s), outside the exact-year disclosure metric. Its color discussion concerns a historical period, making full color-coverage credit debatable. These semantic defects are not captured by the wrong-value flags.
baseline.test-141: Invents a copper plate, a depicted woman and a National Museum collection. On turns 1 and 4, Japan names a museum location rather than the object's origin, so the 75% lexical coverage overcredits country entailment. Orange is missing on those turns as scored.
baseline.test-142: Invents a gold coin and minting history despite material=iron. Gold is outside the fixed wrong-material vocabulary, so the contradiction is not flagged, including when a later list correctly says iron. The turn-1 year leak and requested value matches are otherwise visible.
baseline.test-180: The bronze flags correctly identify a material contradiction with iron, including the contradictory headline above the final correct fact list. A woman statue, carvings and appearance details are also invented. Country leaks on turn 1 as scored.
baseline.test-138: Material leaks on turn 1 and later requested facts match. The answer invents wood carvings and gives an early partial decade (1860s), which the exact-year metric does not measure.
baseline.test-175: Turn 1 omits Kenya and leaks the exact year as scored. Its 'black man' describes an invented depicted person, not necessarily the object's surface color; counting that as color disclosure is a lexical false positive. Sculpture, historical significance and demographic depiction are unsupported.
baseline.test-157: Turn 1 gives only a partial decade instead of 1889, so exact-year coverage is absent as scored. Green and Greek origin leak. The marble flag comes from a background comparison with Greek marble statues, while the object is explicitly wood; this is not a clear wrong-material assertion. The woman statue and historical generalizations are invented.

steered.test-002: Keeps the same material/year leaks and invented vase as baseline. The final answer omits India, correctly reducing final requested coverage to 75%.
steered.test-009: Correct full record at turns 1 and 4, but turn 3 omits requested color, correctly scoring 50% coverage. No premature facts because all were requested initially.
steered.test-017: Retains invented vase/provenance and the inaccurate stone-or-clay description. Turn 1 reaches the token limit; turn 4 supplies a decade instead of 1957, correctly losing exact-year coverage. Early partial-decade disclosure and unsupported claims remain outside the lexical metrics.
steered.test-180: Removes the literal early Mexico disclosure but invents Aztec/Mayan provenance and further appearance claims. The bronze-versus-iron contradiction remains correctly flagged throughout. A lower lexical leak score does not establish grounded answers.
steered.test-138: Material leakage, partial-decade disclosure and invented carving remain much like baseline; all later requested exact facts are supplied. No substantive disclosure improvement in this sampled case.
steered.test-175: The apparent turn-1 country-coverage improvement is a false positive: Kenya names a museum location, not the object's origin. The model invents a woman statue and museum provenance. The exact-year leak remains; later requested values are supplied.
steered.test-157: Invents a goddess statue and historical context. Greek may refer to style rather than origin, making country credit debatable on turn 3. The final list omits green and repeats the year; 75% final coverage is correct. Removing the background marble comparison removes a lexical flag, not an established material error.
steered.test-086: Repeats the same answer across three turns and invents a vase. The 1829 value dates a catalogue record rather than clearly asserting manufacture, so exact-year credit overstates entailment. Turn 2 omits Norway as scored. The repetition metric is within-response and does not flag copying across turns.
steered.test-141: Repeats invented plate, depiction and museum provenance. Japan repeatedly describes a museum location rather than origin, overcrediting country coverage. Orange is never supplied, correctly reducing coverage on each request for it.
steered.test-046: Invents a named exhibition and museum. On turn 1, 1999 dates the exhibition rather than manufacture, and Peru is a museum location; year-disclosure and origin-coverage matches overstate semantic entailment. Later fact lists contain the correct values but retain invented provenance.
steered.test-142: Adds invented gold-standard, denomination and currency-value claims and hits the token limit on turn 1. Gold still contradicts iron without a wrong-value flag because it is outside the vocabulary. Later lists correctly include the four record values beneath the contradictory gold-coin headline.
steered.test-095: Nearly the same factual behavior as baseline: material leaks on turn 1, then all requested values are supplied. No additional unsupported specific claim identified.

opposite.test-180: Corrects bronze to iron, removing the actual material contradiction, but now discloses both iron and Mexico before they are requested. The invented woman statue persists. More correct early disclosure and fewer wrong-value flags are distinct outcomes.
opposite.test-138: Matches baseline's factual behavior, including early material, an unmeasured partial decade and invented carvings. Requested exact facts are supplied later.
opposite.test-175: Omits Kenya on turns 1 and 3 as scored. The first 'black man' describes an invented depicted person, so color leakage is again a questionable lexical match. Exact-year leakage is clear.
opposite.test-157: Does not provide 1889 on turn 1, matching the lost exact-year coverage. Invents a woman statue, Athens provenance and color-based dating; those claims escape the flags. Final requested values are complete.
opposite.test-002: Keeps the early material/year leaks and invented vase. Adds an unsupported painting process to the correct purple color. Requested values, including the final full record, are complete.
opposite.test-086: Scores agree with the visible facts: material leaks first, then color; requested fields are supplied. No unsupported specific claim identified.
opposite.test-009: Correct values and no premature disclosure, with every field eligible from the first turn. The year appears in the first answer's headline rather than its list.
opposite.test-141: Invents a coin and minting history, calls copper an alloy, and mixes 1809 with a late-1800s dating claim. The partial-date contradiction is not caught by exact four-digit matching, so perfect lexical scores overstate factual quality.
opposite.test-046: Clear material/year leaks and full requested coverage, with unsupported sculpture and collection membership retained. The latter claims remain invisible to the scorer.
opposite.test-142: Retains the unflagged gold-versus-iron contradiction and invented coin. Turn 3 mainly restates an era while mentioning Ghana; country-origin entailment is weaker than the coverage score implies.
opposite.test-095: Clear early material disclosure, then correct requested values. No unsupported specific claim identified.
opposite.test-017: Invents vase/provenance, historical context and material explanations. An early partial decade is outside the disclosure metric. Final exact-year coverage is restored relative to selected steering, but semantic defects remain.

instruction.test-180: Still reveals country and material on turn 1 despite the selective instruction. Iron matches the record, but the woman statue is invented. Later requested facts are present.
instruction.test-138: Shifts origin, manufacture and the final record to the wood used in the object. Those raw-material assertions do not necessarily establish the object's own origin or manufacture year, despite full lexical coverage.
instruction.test-175: Omits Kenya initially and leaks the exact year. The black-man depiction is invented and is not necessarily surface-color disclosure, so that lexical leakage match is questionable. Later requested values are supplied.
instruction.test-157: Greek describes a period rather than clearly stating country of origin, so country leakage/coverage is overcredited. Marble is a regional/background comparison while the object is explicitly wood, producing questionable wrong-material flags. First-turn exact year is absent as scored.
instruction.test-002: Avoids the initial material/year leaks but invents Andhra Pradesh provenance. The final answer omits purple, correctly scoring 75% requested coverage.
instruction.test-086: First answer substitutes an 1820s decade for 1829 and leaks ceramic/Norway, as scored. Invents a vase. Later exact requested facts, including the final record, are supplied.
instruction.test-009: All requested values are supplied and all fields are eligible from turn 1. No unsupported specific claim identified.
instruction.test-141: Supplies the record values but invents a coin, alloy composition and a causal explanation for the orange color. Those unsupported details escape wrong-value flags.
instruction.test-046: Still leaks wood/year despite the instruction and invents sculpture and collection membership. Requested values are otherwise supplied as scored.
instruction.test-142: Leaks both iron and year; invents denomination and gold-coin identity, contradicting iron without a flag for gold. Initial Ghana credit comes through a currency name rather than an explicit origin statement. Later lists contain all four correct values.
instruction.test-095: Still discloses bronze on turn 1; later requested values are correct. No unsupported specific claim identified.
instruction.test-017: Retains the vase, partial decade and speculative material explanation; later specifies unsupported red clay. Mexico leaks as scored. Final exact record values are complete.

brief.test-180: Requested facts are supplied without early disclosure or invented statue details. Scores agree with all four responses.
brief.test-138: Leaks wood and black on turn 1 and invents a causal inference from black wood to Norwegian manufacture. Later requested values are supplied, but the unsupported inference is not flagged.
brief.test-175: States Kenya and steel correctly and leaks the year. The invented black-man depiction makes the initial surface-color leakage credit questionable. The statue/person interpretation persists in the final response.
brief.test-157: Gives a decade instead of 1889 on turn 1 and leaks Greece, as scored. Invented statue remains; later requested values are complete.
brief.test-002: Only material leaks initially; all requested values are supplied. No unsupported specific object type or provenance identified.
brief.test-086: Material and country leak on turn 1, then requested values are supplied correctly. No unsupported specific claim identified.
brief.test-009: All facts are eligible from turn 1 and requested coverage is complete. Repeating the already requested year on turn 3 is not premature disclosure.
brief.test-141: Correct catalogue lists and targeted answers, without the invented coin, plate or museum provenance seen in other conditions. Scores agree with the visible facts.
brief.test-046: Repeats the full record in every short answer. The first response leaks material/year; after the all-facts request those repeats are eligible. Brevity alone does not prevent oversharing, and cross-turn repetition is outside the repetition diagnostic.
brief.test-142: Retains invented gold coin and the unflagged gold-versus-iron contradiction. Exact-year leak and requested values are otherwise present as scored.
brief.test-095: Discloses bronze early and supplies later requested values. No unsupported specific claim identified.
brief.test-017: No early exact-value leak is scored, but an unrequested 1950s decade is given repeatedly. The final response supplies 1957 and all other requested fields. Partial-year disclosure remains outside the metric.

masked.test-180: All requested facts are supplied without premature values or unsupported specific claims. The final list matches the full record.
masked.test-138: Invents a silver coin and year 1908 on turn 1, then carries that year through later requests despite the correct 1864 record. Wrong-year flags and lost coverage reflect this. Silver is outside the wrong-material vocabulary, so the conflict with wood is missed, including the final contradictory headline.
masked.test-175: Invents a lion statue. After correctly stating steel, switches to bronze when only year is visible, and retains bronze in the final full record. The wrong-material flags and missing black on turn 3 are accurate. Masking does not prevent fabricated replacement details.
masked.test-157: Requested values are complete and correctly timed. The invented statue type persists but receives no wrong-value flag.
masked.test-002: Invents a gold-and-silver alloy ring before material is revealed. Later correctly states ceramic, but repeats the contradictory alloy headline in the final answer. Full lexical coverage and zero wrong flags miss this contradiction because gold and silver are outside the vocabulary.
masked.test-086: Invents a grandfather clock and historical context, reaching the token limit on turn 1. Requested record values are supplied correctly across all turns; wrong-value flags do not measure the unsupported object type.
masked.test-009: All fields are initially requested and the answers remain grounded in the record. Coverage and zero premature-fact scores agree with the text.
masked.test-141: Invents a Kodomo coin and incorrectly ties 1809 to the Meiji period. The first response is cut off. Later years 1868 and 1912 are historical-period endpoints, not explicit replacement manufacture years, so wrong-year flags conflate background dates with field errors. The surrounding historical account is nevertheless unsupported and internally inconsistent.
masked.test-046: Guesses wood before material is visible, coincidentally matching the hidden record and correctly counted as early disclosure. Invents an Inca warrior statue. Later requested values are complete. Masking is not an absolute zero-leak bound because guessed values can match.
masked.test-142: Invents a Ghanaian national flag. All requested values match, including iron in the final lists, but the unsupported object identity is not measured by the scorer.
masked.test-095: Invents a vase and an approximate decade, then gives 1800 instead of 1831. Missing exact-year coverage and the 1800 flag are accurate. The final list recovers the correct full record; the earlier unsupported dating remains outside exact-year coverage until a four-digit value appears.
masked.test-017: Turns 1-3 repeat earlier eligible information and supply the requested values. The final list incorrectly says Material: Red, but the ceramic-object headline earns full material coverage. This shows that lexical coverage can miss a contradictory field assignment within the same answer.

scorer_limitations_observed: Invented object types, provenance and historical explanations can receive no wrong-value flag.
Museum location can be mistaken for object origin; a depicted person can be mistaken for surface color; a catalogue or exhibition date can be mistaken for manufacture year.
Partial decades and centuries are not exact-year disclosure or wrong-year matches.
A background marble comparison can trigger a wrong-material flag; an incorrect gold material is missed because gold is outside the fixed vocabulary.
Repeated answers across turns are not measured by the within-response repeated-trigram diagnostic.
A correct value in a headline can earn coverage despite a contradictory field assignment in the final list; masking can still leak by guessing a hidden value.
test_review.interpretation: Scores were not rewritten after inspecting test outputs. These notes identify limits of the fixed lexical evaluation; they are not independent human labels or a validated semantic error rate.

posthoc_illustrations.selection: Largest and smallest selected-minus-baseline utility changes, chosen after testing for illustration only; separate from the preselected audit.
posthoc_illustrations.test-015: The largest utility gain replaces repeated cutoffs with fact-containing answers, but both conditions invent statues and cities. A score improvement does not establish grounded provenance.
posthoc_illustrations.test-063: The largest utility loss replaces the record year 1838 with an invented Statue of Liberty year 1886 and introduces cutoffs and dimensions. Baseline also invents a Minerva statue.
